history.heading: The Clunies-Ross kingdom
paragraphs: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are two coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, roughly halfway between Australia and Sri Lanka. Captain William Keeling sighted them in 1609, but they remained uninhabited until 1826.

Scottish trader John Clunies-Ross settled there in 1827 with workers brought mainly from the Malay world to establish coconut plantations. Britain annexed the islands in 1857, and in 1886 Queen Victoria granted them to the Clunies-Ross family, who ran them as a private fiefdom for over a century, paying workers in their own token currency. During the First World War, the German cruiser Emden was destroyed nearby.

history.heading: Australian rule
paragraphs: The islands were transferred to Australia in 1955. Australia bought out the Clunies-Ross family in 1978, and in a UN-supervised act of self-determination in 1984, residents voted to integrate with Australia.

culture.heading: Cocos Malay community
paragraphs: Most residents live on Home Island and are Cocos Malays, descendants of the plantation workers, who are mainly Sunni Muslim and speak a distinctive Malay dialect. A smaller community, mostly European Australians, lives on West Island. Traditional boat building and festivals such as Hari Raya are important.

politics.heading: Australian external territory
paragraphs: The islands are an Australian external territory administered by an administrator appointed by the Australian government, with a local shire council. Residents vote in Australian federal elections.

economy.heading: Small island economy
paragraphs: The economy is very small, based on government services, tourism (diving, fishing and kitesurfing) and some coconut products. Most goods are imported. An airstrip on West Island is being upgraded for Australian defence use. The currency is the Australian dollar.
